concept_note.title: Linear Algebra: Vectors
concept_note.summary: A vector is a list of numbers that represents something. Every AI model is built out of vectors and the simple operations between them.
learning_goals: See how vectors represent real things (images, words, features)
Add vectors and multiply by a scalar
Understand why AI uses vectors everywhere
concept_note.long_intro: If you remember one idea from AI mathematics, make it this: everything is a vector. An image is a vector of pixel intensities. A word is a vector of learned numbers. A user is a vector of preferences. A model's internal state is a vector. Once you see the world as vectors, most AI becomes a matter of moving vectors around in space. This lesson introduces vectors without any math anxiety — we will build them from everyday examples, and you will see that the operations between vectors are exactly what you would expect.

deep_explanation.heading: What a vector is
deep_explanation.body: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. That is it. [3, 5, 2] is a vector. [0.5, -0.2, 0.8, 1.0] is a vector. The length of the list is called the vector's dimension. A 3-dimensional vector has three numbers, a 100-dimensional vector has one hundred. In AI, vectors typically have hundreds or thousands of dimensions because they are representing complex things. Do not let the high dimension scare you — the operations are the same whether you have 3 numbers or 3000.
deep_explanation.code:
v = [3, 5, 2]
print(len(v))    # shows 3
print(v[0])      # shows 3
print(v[2])      # shows 2

deep_explanation.heading: Vectors represent real things
deep_explanation.body: A vector becomes meaningful when we decide what each number means. A grayscale image of 28 by 28 pixels is naturally a vector of 784 numbers, each one a brightness value between 0 and 255. A user's movie preferences could be a vector where each number is a rating of a different genre. A word in a language model becomes a vector where each number captures some learned aspect of its meaning. The vector itself is just numbers. The meaning comes from what the numbers represent.
deep_explanation.code:
# An image as a vector (simplified: 4 pixels)
image = [12, 240, 87, 155]
print("pixel values:", image)

deep_explanation.heading: Adding vectors and scaling them
deep_explanation.body: Two operations you will see constantly: adding two vectors (element by element) and multiplying a vector by a single number (called a scalar). Adding [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] gives [5, 7, 9]. Multiplying [1, 2, 3] by 2 gives [2, 4, 6]. These two operations are the atoms of every neural network. When a network combines information from two sources, it adds the vectors. When it amplifies a signal, it scales by a scalar. Once you can add and scale vectors, you can read most of what a neural network is doing at the arithmetic level.
deep_explanation.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [4, 5, 6]
sum_vec = [a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1], a[2] + b[2]]
print(sum_vec)   # shows [5, 7, 9]

scaled = [2 * x for x in a]
print(scaled)    # shows [2, 4, 6]

concept_note.formal_definition: A vector is an element of R^n for some dimension n, written as an ordered tuple of n real numbers. The two fundamental operations are addition (element-wise) and scalar multiplication. The set of all n-dimensional vectors with these operations forms a vector space. Distance between vectors is measured by norms; similarity is measured by the dot product.

code_example.code:
user_a = [5, 3, 1]   # ratings for three genres
user_b = [4, 2, 2]

combined = [user_a[i] + user_b[i] for i in range(3)]
print(combined)   # shows [9, 5, 3]

scaled = [2 * x for x in user_a]
print(scaled)     # shows [10, 6, 2]
code_example.universal_explanation: Two users are each represented by a 3-dimensional vector of ratings. Adding the vectors gives a combined preference profile. Scaling one user's vector by 2 doubles all their ratings. Both operations work element by element.

common_mistakes: Adding vectors of different lengths: [1, 2] + [1, 2, 3] is not defined. Both vectors must have the same dimension.
Confusing the dimension with the number of vectors: a vector of dimension 5 has 5 numbers; it is still one vector.
Thinking that [1, 2, 3] and [3, 2, 1] are the same vector: order matters. Vectors are ordered.
Assuming that multiplying a vector by 2 changes only the first element: scalar multiplication applies to every element.
concept_note.real_world_usage: In recommendation systems like Netflix, every user is a vector of preferences and every movie is a vector of features. The system recommends movies whose vectors are close to the user's vector. In image recognition, every image is flattened into a vector before entering the network. In language models, every word becomes a vector called an embedding. The reason vectors are universal is that they let you compare, combine, and transform information using simple operations.
key_takeaways: A vector is an ordered list of numbers.
The dimension is how many numbers the vector contains.
Vectors represent anything we choose to encode as numbers.
Adding vectors is element by element.
Multiplying by a scalar affects every element.

activity.question: What is [3, 6, 9] multiplied by 3?
activity.reveal: Multiplying by a scalar affects every element: 3*3=9, 6*3=18, 9*3=27.

test.prompt: Why do AI models use vectors instead of storing data as tables or lists of separate values?
test.rubric: Should mention that vectors let us do math on data (add, scale, compare), and that this is what neural networks require.
